senses.def: to provide otherwise unknown information

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to not being in accordance with what is right, appropriate, or fitting
pertaining to having been proven worthless
the state of being taken as a prisoner of war and kept a captive
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be necessary to render ‘captivity’ in terms of ‘being a captive,’ and therefore this expression in Revelation 13:10 may be rendered as ‘if anyone is meant to become a captive, he will indeed become a captive.’

senses.def: to grind grain in a mill
senses.comment: In Luke 17:35 and also in Matthew 24:41 the reference is evidently to a hand mill, which was normally operated by two women working together. In societies in which such mills are not known, translators have frequently substituted the process of pounding grain by means of a mortar and pestle.

senses.def: (derivative of ἄμπελος ‘grapevine’) a field or garden of grapevines, creeping plants that develop a woody stem when they mature; Vitis vinifera; they grow along the ground until they find a tree or other object to climb, using tendrils; they bear bunches of small round fruit that are sweet and juicy; a symbol of blessing, prosperity, and happiness
senses.comment: In some instances a vineyard may be described as ‘a farm with grapevines’ or ‘a garden for grapes.’

senses.def: to conduct a judicial inquiry
pertaining to what can be borne or endured
senses.comment: In some languages ‘it will be more tolerable’ in Matthew 11:22 may be satisfactorily expressed as ‘it will be easier to bear’ or ‘the suffering will be less.’

senses.def: to oppose someone, involving not only a psychological attitude but also a corresponding behavior
(derivative of ἀπειθέω[a] ‘to disobey,’ 36.23) pertaining to being continuously disobedient
(derivative of ἀποκρίνομαι[a] ‘to reply,’ 33.184) that which is said in response to a question

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to behaving in an unprejudiced manner
a relatively small and generally round loaf of bread (considerably smaller than present-day typical loaves of bread and thus more like rolls or buns)
any kind of food or nourishment
senses.comment: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as Matthew 6:11 as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering Luke 4:4 (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of Luke 4:4 is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: bread of the placing forth) bread which was set out as an offering in the presence of God in the Tabernacle and later in the Temple
senses.comment: In some languages ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως is rendered as ‘bread placed before God’ or ‘bread placed in the presence of God.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to break bread) to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
senses.comment: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.|The implication of ‘eating together’ comes from the total context. ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων συνηγμένων ἡμῶν κλάσαι ἄρτον ‘on the first day of the week we gathered together for a meal’ Acts 20:7. No doubt the reference in Acts 20:7 is to the ‘fellowship meal,’ called ‘agape,’ which constituted the early Christian form of the ‘Lord’s Supper.’ See 23.28.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to eat one’s own bread) to earn a living by one’s own efforts
a state of safety and security, implying a complete lack of danger
senses.comment: In some languages safety or security is expressed in a negative way, for example, ‘without any danger’ or ‘without anything that might possibly harm.’

senses.def: a state of certainty with regard to a belief
senses.comment: It is also possible to render Luke 1:4 as ‘so that you may know that those things that you have been taught are certainly true.’

senses.subdomain: Enjoy, Take Pleasure In, Be Fond of Doing
senses.def: pertaining to not being desirous or greedy for money
glosses: one who does not love money

senses.def: (derivative of βασανίζω ‘to torture,’ 38.13) a person serving as a guard in a prison, whose function was to torture prisoners as a phase of judicial examination
senses.comment: It is difficult to know in the case of Matthew 18:34 if βασανιστής is to be understood in the specific sense of ‘torturer’ (in which case it could be classified after 38.13) or only in terms of ‘prison guard.’ The use of βασανιστής in Matthew 18:34 may simply be an instance of literary hyperbole. As such it may be possible to translate the expression in Matthew 18:34 as ‘his master was very angry and handed him over to prison guards to torture him until he should pay back the whole amount.’

senses.def: to cause harm or injury to someone or something (a highly generic meaning involving a wide range of harm and injury)
senses.comment: In translating terms meaning ‘to harm’ or ‘to injure,’ it may be necessary to specify suffering, for example, ‘to cause people to suffer’ or ‘to cause people to have pain.’

senses.def: a city in southwest Palestine on a principal road to Egypt
to possess information about
to cause information to be known by someone
pertaining to being cowardly
senses.comment: In some languages a ‘coward’ is ‘one who always runs’ or ‘one who runs away at nothing.’

senses.def: to express discontent in an emphatic way
(derivative of διατάσσω[a] ‘to order, to instruct,’ 33.325) that which has been specifically ordered or commanded
a joint name for Castor and Pollux, pagan deities of an Alexandrian ship
pertaining to being difficult to explain or interpret
a set of religious beliefs and practices resulting from one’s own desires and initiative
to give justice to someone who has been wronged
to repay harm with harm, on the assumption that the initial harm was unjustified and that retribution is therefore called for
to punish, on the basis of what is rightly deserved
(derivative of ἐκτείνω ‘to stretch out,’ 16.19) pertaining to an unceasing activity, normally involving a degree of intensity and/or perseverance
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐκτενῶς in Acts 12:5, see 25.71.

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: pertaining to being eager to persevere in some state or activity
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐκτενῶς in Acts 12:5, see ἐκτενῶς[a] 68.12.

senses.def: a magician of Cyprus
to put on clothes, without implying any particular article of clothing
to ask for something and to receive what one has asked for

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: to give or commit oneself wholeheartedly to something
senses.comment: In a number of languages the concept of ‘devoting oneself to’ or ‘giving oneself wholly to’ is often expressed as ‘to do with one’s whole heart’ or ‘to want to do nothing else but.’

senses.def: to happen in conjunction with some other happening
glosses: to happen at the same time

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to follow in the tracks) to behave in the same manner as someone else
placing something on something
to cause to come together to, toward, or at a particular location
to come or gather together to, toward, or at a particular location
to move from one place to another, either coming or going
senses.comment: Note that in Mark 4:21 the subject of ἔρχεται is not something that would normally move by its own force but would need to be brought. Accordingly, in a number of languages it is necessary to say ‘no one brings a lamp …’

senses.def: to move toward or up to the reference point of the viewpoint character or event
to come into a particular state or condition, implying a process
to happen, with the implication of the event being directed to someone or something
(an idiom, literally: to come into) to result in a state

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to come in sheeps clothing) to pretend to be harmless when in reality one is dangerous and destructive
senses.comment: In many languages it is possible to retain the idiom ἔρχομαι ἐν ἐνδύμασιν προβάτων, since the context seems to explain rather clearly what is meant. However, in a number of languages it may be necessary to translate ἔρχομαι ἐν ἐνδύμασιν προβάτων as ‘to come looking like sheep’ or ‘to come looking as innocent as sheep.’

senses.def: to consider a view favorably, with the intention of finding a solution
glosses: to consider someone’s views in a favorable light
senses.comment: For other interpretations of εὐνοέω in Matthew 5:25, see 31.20 and 56.3.

senses.def: to come to an agreement with someone
senses.comment: For other interpretations of εὐνοέω in Matthew 5:25, see 30.23 and 56.3.

senses.def: to settle a case out of court
senses.comment: For other interpretations of εὐνοέω in Matthew 5:25, see 30.23 and 31.20.

senses.def: a chief tax collector of Jericho
a person greeted in Romans 16:11
(derivative of Θεσσαλονίκη ‘Thessalonica,’ 93.475) a person who lives in or is a native of Thessalonica

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: jasper; probably green in color (see 2.29)

large domesticated solid-hoofed quadruped; Equus caballus; stockily built in comparison to today’s horses, with shorter heads and thicker necks; about 122–142 cm tall, and 2.1 m long; coat varies from dark to pale brown; eats plants; used in battle, both to ride and for pulling chariots; symbolic of military might; associated with the sun, which was said to ride across the sky in a chariot
senses.comment: Since horses are widely distributed in the world (at least knowledge about them is widespread), it is rarely difficult to obtain a satisfactory term. In some instances, however, expressions designating horses may seem rather strange. For example, in Sediq, a language spoken in Taiwan, a horse is literally ‘a soldier’s cow.’

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: pertaining to recurring on a daily basis

(a figurative extension of meaning of καρδία ‘heart,’ not occurring in the NT in its literal sense) the causative source of a person’s psychological life in its various aspects, but with special emphasis upon thoughts
senses.comment: It is often possible to render καρδία[a] by a number of different terms depending upon the immediate context, for example, ‘mind,’ ‘intention,’ ‘purpose,’ or ‘desire.’ In many languages it is quite impossible to use a term meaning ‘heart,’ since such a term may not lend itself to figurative extension in meaning. Often the equivalent of καρδία is ‘liver,’ while in a number of languages it is ‘stomach’ or ‘bowels.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of καρδία ‘heart,’ not occurring in the NT in its literal sense) a location deep within a larger area
(an idiom, literally: to pierce the heart) to experience acute emotional distress, implying both concern and regret
(an idiom, literally: to convince the heart) to exhibit confidence and assurance in a situation which might otherwise cause dismay or fear
(an idiom, literally: to maim the heart) to cause someone to be unwilling to learn
glosses: to make someone unable to learn
senses.comment: This expression is only found as a variant reading: πεπήρωκεν αὐτῶν τὴν καρδίαν ‘he has made their hearts unable to learn’ John 12:40 (apparatus).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to broaden the heart) to make evident that one has affection for someone
(an idiom, literally: to fill the heart, and: to throw into the heart) to cause someone to think in a particular manner, often as a means of inducing some behavior

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to be sprinkled in the heart) to be purified from moral failure
glosses: to have one’s heart made pure
to be purified in one’s heart

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to break the heart) to cause great sorrow and grief
senses.comment: It is rare that one can reproduce in a literal form the idiom συνθρύπτω τὴν καρδίαν. A frequent equivalent of ‘to break one’s heart’ is ‘to cause one to cry.’ In some languages one may even have ‘to cause one’s heart to cry.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to place in the heart) to store information in the mind, with the implication of its being valuable
glosses: to treasure up in the heart
to store in the mind as valuable

senses.def: pertaining to the part of a whole which remains or continues, and thus constitutes the rest of the whole
(derivative of εἴδωλον[a] ‘idol,’ 6.97) pertaining to numerous idols, objects (not necessarily three-dimensional) formed to resemble a person, god, animal, etc.
senses.comment: In place of the traditional rendering ‘how full of idols their city was,’ one may have ‘how many idols there were in their city’ or ‘how many idols the people worshiped there in their city.’

senses.def: coins of lesser value
(an idiom, literally: to itch with respect to hearing) to have one’s ears tickled by what is heard
glosses: to desire to hear what one wants to hear

senses.def: to shout or cry out, with the possible implication of the unpleasant nature of the sound

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a title of respect used in addressing or speaking of a woman
senses.comment: It is likely, however, that κυρία in 2 John 1:1 refers to the church as a lady.

senses.def: (derivative of Λευί ‘Levi,’ son of Jacob, 93.231) pertaining to being a descendant of Levi
senses.comment: The phrase ‘through the Levitical priesthood’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘by those priests who were descended from Levi.’

senses.def: (derivative of λυτρόω ‘to liberate,’ 37.128) a person who liberates or releases others
senses.comment: The phrase ‘ruler and liberator’ may, of course, be expressed by a verbal form, for example, ‘as one who is to rule over you and to set you free.’

senses.def: to make a serious declaration on the basis of presumed personal knowledge
to be emphatic in stating an opinion or desire
(derivative of μεσιτεύω ‘to bring about an agreement,’ 31.21) one who causes or helps parties to come to an agreement, with the implication of guaranteeing the certainty of the arrangement
a person who acts as a mediator in bringing about reconciliation
senses.comment: A mediator may be spoken of in a number of different ways, often idiomatically, for example, ‘one who stands in the middle,’ ‘one who speaks to both,’ ‘one who cuts palavers,’ or ‘one who causes arguments to cease.’ It is also possible, however, to regard μεσίτης as being related to the process of causing agreement between the parties in question. For this aspect of the meaning of μεσίτης, see 31.22.

senses.def: one’s biological or adoptive female parent
senses.comment: μήτηρ[a] is sometimes used figuratively to refer to persons who are not biological parents but who are in some respects closely associated with the reference person: μήτηρ μου καὶ ἀδελφοί μου οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ ἀκούοντες καὶ ποιοῦντες ‘my mother and my brothers are those who hear God’s word and act accordingly’ Luke 8:21. For a discussion of Luke 8:21, see 10.49.

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of μήτηρ[a] ‘mother,’ 10.16) an archetype anticipating a later reality and suggesting a derivative relationship
(derivative of μύλος[a] ‘mill,’ 7.68) pertaining to a stone mill for grinding grain
senses.comment: The translation of such adjectival forms depends upon specific contexts. There is, of course, no need to translate an adjectival form by a corresponding adjective in a receptor language, especially when a noun would be more appropriate.

senses.def: to go without food for a set time as a religious duty
the state of being very hungry, presumably for a considerable period of time and as the result of necessity rather than choice (compare νηστεία[a] ‘fasting,’ 53.65)
senses.comment: Terms referring to hunger often distinguish varying degrees of hunger and whether the hunger is by necessity or by choice.

senses.def: a Jewish festival celebrating the forgiveness of sins on the day of atonement
glosses: day to commemorate the atonement of sin
senses.comment: The Day of Atonement in the Jewish calendar occurs in the fall, a time which is particularly dangerous to small ships in the Mediterranean. In biblical times, small merchant ships normally stayed in a harbor over the winter months.

senses.def: (derivative of ξύλον[a] ‘wood,’ 3.60) pertaining to being made or consisting of wood
an animal which has been sacrificed to God and completely burned up on the altar

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a relative state of anger
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘anger’ without indicating against whom the anger exists. For example, in 1 Timothy 2:8 it might be possible to say ‘to pray without anger against anyone’ or ‘to pray without being angry at anyone.’

senses.def: divine punishment based on God’s angry judgment against someone
senses.comment: Though the focal semantic element in ὀργή[b] is punishment, at the same time there is an implication of God’s anger because of evil. Therefore, it is possible in some languages to translate this expression in Romans 3:5 as ‘God does not do wrong when he is angry and punishes us, does he?’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of οὖς[a] ‘ear,’ 8.24) the activity of hearing

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: (idioms, literally: into the ear, and: to the ear) pertaining to what is known only by those who hear a particular message in private
senses.comment: A phrase such as ‘whatever you hear in secret’ may be rendered as ‘whatever you hear when no one else is listening.’|For another treatment of the phrase πρὸς τὸ οὖς λαλέω, see 33.91.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to speak to the ear) to speak quietly and presumably to a restricted audience
senses.comment: For another treatment of the phrase πρὸς τὸ οὖς, see 28.73.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: hold the ears closed) to refuse to listen to what is being said
senses.comment: In some languages the refusal to hear may be expressed idiomatically as ‘they put their hands over their ears’ or ‘they closed their ears’ or ‘the words never entered their heads.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to put into the ears) to listen carefully to, with the implication of not forgetting
senses.comment: For another interpretation of this idiom in Luke 9:44, see 29.5.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to place in the ears) to continue to bear something in mind
senses.comment: For another interpretation of the idiom τίθεμαι εἰς τὰ ὦτα in Luke 9:44, see 24.64.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to hear heavily with the ears) to be mentally slow or dull in comprehending

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: duration of time, with reference to a series of occasions
to give or to provide for, with the implication of placing something in front of a person, normally food
an idiom, literally: to place alongside a parable
to entrust oneself to the care of someone
glosses: to commit oneself to the care of

senses.def: to establish evidence to show that something is true
pertaining to teaching which has been handed down from the ancestors

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: to cause something not to be known
a relatively flat, large dish; made of baked clay or metal
(derivative of ποιέω[e] ‘to make,’ 42.29) that which is made
an interrogative reference to a position
a relative reference to a set of circumstances
(an idiom, literally: where will it appear) a question as to what may have happened to someone or something
to make ready or prepare in advance
to express by attitude and possibly by position one’s allegiance to and regard for deity

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.subdomain: Prostrate as an Act of Reverence or Supplication
senses.def: to prostrate oneself before someone as an act of reverence, fear, or supplication
senses.comment: προσκυνέω[b] is semantically very complex in that it indicates not only a body position but also an attitude and activity of reverence or honor. In many contexts it is not necessary to specify both semantic elements, but one or the other may be selected depending upon what seems to be the focus of attention. For example, in Mark 15:19 one may either translate ‘they knelt before him and worshiped him in a mocking way’ or ‘they knelt before him and prostrated themselves before him.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the back part of the human foot below the ankle
senses.comment: πτέρνα occurs in the NT only in John 13:18 (ὁ τρώγων μου τὸν ἄρτον ἐπῆρεν ἐπ᾽ ἐμὲ τὴν πτέρναν αὐτοῦ ‘the one eating my bread has raised his heel against me’) in an idiomatic expression denoting antagonism and opposition (see 39.3).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to lift one’s heel against) to oppose someone by turning against such a person, possibly with focus upon the initial aspect of becoming opposed to
senses.comment: In a number of languages a convenient way of rendering ‘to turn against’ may be ‘to become an enemy of.’|πτέρνα occurs in the NT only in John 13:18 in an idiomatic expression denoting antagonism and opposition.

senses.def: the wife of Isaac
a major OT prophet

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a cloth or piece of leather wrapped by a workman around his waist or chest to protect his clothes
senses.comment: A σιμικίνθιον may be called in some languages ‘a workman’s cloth’ or ‘a workman’s cloth to protect clothing.’

senses.def: a stretcher or plank used for carrying a corpse to a place of burial

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to be in a standing position
to continue in a state, with a possible implication of acceptability
senses.comment: For a discussion of στήκω as part of an idiom in Romans 14:4, see 87.56.

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to his own master he stands or falls, probably a familiar adage) whether one maintains one’s status or relationship to a master depends on the masters judgment or evaluation
glosses: honor or disgrace depends on the person whom one serves

senses.def: to live in association with or together with someone else
senses.comment: In 2 Corinthians 7:3 it is important to note that συζάω should not be understood in the sense of inhabiting the same house with someone else. The reference here is the sense of unity and comradeship rather than dwelling in the same place.

senses.def: to cause to come together, whether of animate or inanimate objects
to collect and put in a safe place
to convert property or goods into money
the movement of two or more objects to the same location
senses.comment: In a number of languages important distinctions are made in terms referring to gathering or assembling of animate beings. The distinctions are usually based upon the number of individuals, the distance which they have come, and whether or not the individuals in question constitute a membership group or whether they are merely a loose aggregation. In view of these types of distinctions, it is likely that quite different terms will be required for the various contexts listed for this set of related meanings.

senses.def: to acquire information, with focus upon the event of perception
to come to understand clearly on the basis of perceived information
pertaining to divine salvation
the means by which people experience divine salvation
the message about God saving people
an attorney who accused Paul before Felix

(a figurative extension of meaning of τραχηλίζω ‘to have the neck of a sacrificial victim twisted and thus exposed for slaughter,’ not occurring in the NT) that which can readily be known as the result of being exposed

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ὑβρίζω[a] ‘to mistreat with insolence,’ 88.130) one who maltreats others with insolence
senses.comment: It is important to recognize in the term ὑβριστής more than merely an attitude of pride, for ὑβρίζω implies an attitude of superiority which results in mistreatment of and violent acts against others.

senses.def: (derivative of ὑβρίζω[b] to insult, 33.390) one who insults in an arrogant manner
to make known the character or significance of something by visual, auditory, gestural, or linguistic means
senses.comment: In some languages it may be useful to translate ὑποδείκνυμι in Acts 20:35 as ‘I showed you by example’ or ‘I demonstrated by example’ or ‘I showed you by what I did.’

senses.def: to explain the meaning or significance of something by demonstration

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a pompous ceremony, implying a cheap display of high status

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to friendly concern and kindness toward someone
light, in contrast with darkness (σκότος[a], σκοτία[a], 14.53), usually in relationship to some source of light such as the sun, moon, fire, lamp, etc.
senses.comment: Terms for ‘light’ often differ on the basis of whether there is a specific source of light, for example, a fire, lamps, sun, moon, etc., or whether the light is simply generalized, in the sense of daylight apart from the actual shining of the sun (for example, as in the interior of a room). Some languages also make distinctions between terms for light depending on whether the light comes from a fire or lamp or from a heavenly body.|In a number of languages there is no noun for ‘light,’ but only verbs are employed, since the fact of light is spoken of as something which happens and is hence regarded as an event.

senses.def: a pile or heap of burning material
senses.comment: The Greek phrase ἅψαντες … πυράν ‘to kindle a fire’ is best rendered in a number of languages by a single verb meaning ‘to make a fire,’ and in some languages it is strange to speak of a ‘fire’ without indicating the type of material which is being burned. Hence, in Acts 28:2 the appropriate equivalent would be ‘they caused some sticks to burn.’|In some languages a very important distinction is made between two functionally different kinds of fire, one used for getting rid of refuse and the other used for warming oneself. Fire as a destructive agent, mentioned frequently in the book of Revelation (Revelation 8:5 and Revelation 20:10), may require quite a different term from what is used in speaking of a fire for the purpose of warming a person or heating an object.

senses.def: a stick or bundle of sticks carried about as a light
senses.comment: It is, of course, possible that in Acts 16:29 the meaning of φῶς is a lamp (see 6.104).

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (idioms, literally: sons of the light, and: children of light, respectively) persons to whom the truth of God has been revealed and who are presumably living according to such truth. See also 9.4 and 12.15
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of ‘light’ in the metaphorical sense of the truth that comes from God. Such truth is not to be equated with knowledge, but with the principles and practices of right moral behavior. Because of these difficulties in speaking of ‘truth’ as ‘light,’ a number of translators have preferred to use the expression ‘people of God’ for the phrases υἱοὶ τοῦ φωτός, υἱοὶ τῆς ἡμέρας, and τέκνα φωτός. In some instances, however, it is possible to employ ‘light,’ if this is described as ‘light that comes from God’ or even ‘the true light from God.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: in the light) pertaining to being widely known in view of the events in question having taken place in public
to make available whatever is necessary to help or supply the needs of someone
one who habitually engages in gossip
